 The school weathered the storm.
 Twenty years have passed, but I still vividly remember the school that was destroyed after Hurricane Durian, the makeshift classes, and the teachers and friends who helped each other get through those difficult times.
 Báo Tuổi Trẻ • 30/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 A commemorative photo of students from Tan An Luong Secondary School ( Vinh Long province) during the closing ceremony of the 2007-2008 school year - Photo: Nguyen Hieu Nhan
 Twenty years have passed since the historic Typhoon Durian (2006) swept through the South, leaving behind ruined classrooms and books soaked in rain. Amidst the rubble, Tan An Luong Secondary School (Vinh Long province) remains intact in the memories of the 7th grade students.
 After the merger, Tan An Luong Junior High School (Vinh Long province) was renamed Truong Tan Junior High School. Looking back at the school from those days is like a slow-motion film of a time of "school turmoil," a time to appreciate even more the peaceful school we have today.
 The school was a mess of rubble, but the dreams never faded.
 When I was a child, I always thought of school as a place where the doors opened every morning to welcome students, with a bell ringing to signal the start of classes, a blackboard, and chalk.
 School life went on, day after day. I never thought there would be a time when I would go to my familiar classroom and find it no longer intact.
 In December 2006, Typhoon Durian (Typhoon No. 9) swept through southern Vietnam. Tan An Luong Secondary School, where I was studying, suffered heavy damage.
 That year, I was in seventh grade, and my daily worries revolved around homework, assignments, and tests. But after the storm, we had to face something much bigger: the school was destroyed, and we didn't know how we would be able to continue attending classes. 
 Class camping trip in 8th grade, one year after the storm - Photo: NGUYEN HIEU NHAN
 The corrugated iron roofs and rafters of many classroom blocks were blown away by the wind, and the temporary wooden classrooms also collapsed. The school was located in a rural area, and its facilities were very basic at the time. Most of the classrooms were single-story buildings with brick walls and old corrugated iron roofs; the blackboards and teaching materials storage cabinets were all in rooms that were not strong enough to withstand the severe storm.
 The prolonged rain that followed soaked books and papers, damaged desks and chairs, and rendered many items unusable. Seeing this, we were utterly astonished.
 You may also like The place where teachers used to write on the blackboard and students bent their heads to copy notes is now littered with rubble and debris.
 Luckily, students were notified to stay home from school when the storm hit. But just because the storm is over doesn't mean things will go back to normal.
 With a shortage of classrooms, teachers had to coordinate with soldiers, militia, and parents to find temporary learning spaces for students. Some classes had to be held in borrowed spaces, with schedules and sessions changed, and classes combined. 
 Group photo of teachers at the closing ceremony of the 2010-2011 school year - Photo: NGUYEN HIEU NHAN
 The familiar timetable also changed according to the circumstances. We didn't know exactly how the adults managed, but we saw that schooling was still arranged so that we wouldn't have to take too long a break.
 For us seventh-grade students, these changes were both strange and exciting. The immediate concerns were where we would be studying today, what time we should be there, and what books we needed to bring.
 Things weren't the same as before, but we gradually got used to it. Studying in a temporary classroom had its ups and downs. The seating was more cramped, and class schedules had to be divided into shifts. Those with enough supplies shared with their friends; when faced with a difficult problem, the whole group would huddle together to look at it, debating for a while without knowing who was right.
 We still worry when we haven't memorized our lessons, and feel anxious every time there's a test. The storm changed the school buildings, but we're still the same students, with all the little worries typical of schoolchildren.
 Be grateful for the past so you can appreciate the present. 
 Images from the ceremony to receive national standard certification for the school and to celebrate Vietnamese Teachers' Day on November 20, 2013 - Photo: NGUYEN HIEU NHAN
 I am grateful that the teachers still tried to maintain teaching despite the difficult circumstances. They reminded us to take care of our books, sit properly, and concentrate on listening to the lectures.
 The most important thing for the teachers at that time was to quickly repair the damage and arrange for students to return to school. As for us, just having a place to sit and friends by our side was a blessing.
 You may also like The school I used to attend has undergone many changes, renovations, and constructions. Its appearance and rooms today are no longer the same as what I remember from my seventh grade year.
 I am pleased to know that the current students have better learning conditions, sitting in sturdy classrooms. They may not know that the place where they study once experienced a major storm, but I hope they understand that many people have joined hands to help build a well-equipped school like this.
 Twenty years have passed since that storm. Many of the specific events of that time have faded, but I still remember the turmoil in the school after the storm. Back then, we weren't old enough to fully understand the difficulties the adults were facing. We just wanted to go back to school, to see our friends, to sit in our seats again.
 If someone were to ask which school I would still want to name after all these years, I would mention Tan An Luong Junior High School, where the students of that time, despite the difficulties, still bravely came to class every day.
